title: shadow work, minus the jargon
hookLine: TikTok's favorite inner-work word comes from a Swiss psychiatrist, and from an older line about a speck and a beam
carry: what bugs me may be mine
tomorrow: what karma actually keeps track of

lines: THE COWORKER WHO DRIVES YOU UP THE WALL.
cards: Shadow work. Journaling prompts, sixty-second videos, a workbook on every shelf. It sounds dark and a little mystical.
It's neither, exactly. The word comes from a Swiss psychiatrist, and the idea is one you've already lived: the coworker who drives you up the wall for reasons you can't quite name.

teach.h: THE PARTS YOU'D RATHER NOT CLAIM.
teach.b: About a century ago, the psychiatrist Carl Jung used the word shadow for the parts of yourself you'd rather not claim. Not only the ugly bits.
Anger you learned to hide, yes, but also ambition, softness, a talent that didn't fit the family. What we don't own, Jung thought, doesn't disappear.
It tends to show up somewhere else, often in how strongly other people bother us.

He called that projection. The idea is older than him. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus asks: "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?"

teach.h: A SPECK IN THEIRS, A PLANK IN YOURS.
teach.b: A speck in theirs, a plank in yours. So shadow work, minus the jargon, is one simple move.
When someone gets under your skin more than they should, ask: is any of this mine? Not always. Sometimes people really are just annoying.
And the higher self you hear about online is a looser idea, gathered from many places. Jung's own aim was plainer: to become whole, not perfect. For the light version, a notebook is plenty.
For old, heavy pain, a good therapist is better company than any app.

how: People do shadow work with journaling prompts, in therapy (especially with Jungian analysts), and in reflection practices that ask what our strongest reactions to others reveal about ourselves.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the parts you'd rather not claim

s: the shadow is only your dark side
Jung's shadow is whatever you don't claim: hidden anger, and hidden gifts too.
the idea of seeing your own faults in others is older than Jung
Jesus asks why we see the speck in a brother's eye and miss the beam in our own.
shadow work means every annoying person is secretly your fault
not always. the question is whether any of it is yours.

games.q: a coworker's bragging drives you up the wall, much more than it bothers anyone else. what's the shadow-work question?
o: how do I get them to stop?
games.why: a reaction bigger than the thing can be pointing back at you. sometimes it really is just them. it's worth asking.

games.q: put the old picture back together.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of someone who gets under your skin. On the second, name the trait that bugs you, in one word.
On the third, ask, gently, whether any of that word lives in you, hidden or wanted. No verdict needed.

wordCard.voice: The shadow. The parts of you that you'd rather not claim, the dark ones and the bright ones. Sixth word.

carryVoice: Your line: what bugs me may be mine. Not always. Often enough to be worth asking. See you tomorrow.
